public_rationale: OSWorld supports the observation that contemporary agents were error-prone. It does not establish that consumer tasks failed substantially more often than workplace tasks, much less an exponential relationship. Neither benchmark measures consumer tolerance. The evidence therefore supports one component but does not settle the full claim.
limitations: Benchmark tasks do not directly measure production calendar changes or Uber orders.
WorkArena and OSWorld differ in tasks and environments; comparing their headline results would not isolate the effect of a consumer setting.
The period and comparison group require interpretation.

our_interpretation: The claim describes agents available around publication, rather than all future agents. I use April 2024, the latest completed month before the post, for this ongoing technical state.
The surrounding discussion of business automation suggests a comparison with bounded workplace tasks. The speaker does not explicitly identify the comparison group.

The ordinary reading of 'exponentially higher' is a substantially greater risk of failure. A literal exponential relationship would additionally require a specified variable and mathematical relationship.
I read 'less tolerable' as lower user acceptance of failures, which requires evidence about users rather than benchmark scores alone.
criteria.support_condition: Contemporaneous evaluations show frequent agent failures, and comparable consumer and workplace tasks show substantially greater failure risk and lower user tolerance in the consumer setting.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Representative contemporaneous evaluations show dependable agent performance, or matched comparisons show consumer tasks have no greater failure risk or no lower tolerance than the relevant workplace tasks.

Enterprise agents also had substantial limitations. These earlier results caution against assuming workplace automation was a reliable baseline, but cannot establish a matched difference between settings.
